content: The infrastructure and operational requirements for providing lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) to all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV must be thoroughly evaluated. Countries may consider implementing a phased approach, starting with an initial learning phase before scaling up fully. It is essential to establish clear systems for linking patients to care and managing patient transfers. Decisions must be made in advance regarding whether women will continue receiving ART at the same site where antiretroviral (ARV) drugs are provided for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) or if they will be transferred to existing ART sites. Strategies must also be developed to minimize the risk of women being lost to care during these transitions. Human resource requirements must be reviewed, as many staff at PMTCT sites may have limited training and experience in providing ART, particularly in settings where Option A has been implemented for PMTCT. Capacity-building, task shifting, and potentially expanding the health workforce may be necessary to enable PMTCT sites to manage the additional responsibility of providing lifelong ART. Promoting adherence to therapy and retention in care is particularly challenging during the postpartum breastfeeding period. Strategies must be implemented to monitor and support adherence and retention, as well as to re-engage women and their HIV-exposed children who are lost to follow-up. Ethical considerations must be addressed, as initiating lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women, regardless of CD4 count, may create temporary disparities in treatment access. For example, a pregnant woman with a high CD4 count may continue ART after delivery, while her husband or other family members with lower CD4 counts may not yet qualify for treatment. Policies and strategies must be developed to address these disparities and leverage the enrollment of women into lifelong treatment to promote a family-centered approach, including testing and treating partners and other household members. Proper use of testing algorithms is critical for optimal implementation across the country. Laboratory monitoring needs must be assessed. While CD4 testing may not be required to initiate ART in pregnant women, monitoring for ART toxicity and response, including viral load testing to assess viral suppression, should be available for all individuals on ART. Early infant diagnosis is also essential to identify HIV-infected infants and link them to appropriate care and treatment. Surveillance systems should be established to evaluate the impact of ART on birth defects, pregnancy outcomes, and the safety of ART in infants and young children exposed through breastfeeding. Adequate monitoring and evaluation frameworks must be implemented to collect high-quality, longitudinal data on mothers and their HIV-exposed infants across various service delivery points and throughout the continuum of care. Infant prophylaxis is critical in cases of late maternal HIV diagnosis, limited or no maternal ART during pregnancy, or interruptions in maternal ART due to toxicity, intolerance, or non-adherence. Ensuring a continuous drug supply is vital for both PMTCT and maternal health. Accurate drug forecasting and robust supply chain management are essential to prevent stock-outs and treatment interruptions. Countries must carefully consider their PMTCT options, whether to provide ART only during the risk period of mother-to-child transmission (Option B) or to offer lifelong ART regardless of CD4 count (Option B+). The choice should be based on local circumstances, preferences, and values, with attention to contextual factors such as epidemic type, repeat pregnancy rates, access to CD4 testing, and breastfeeding practices. In settings with high fertility rates, family planning programs should be prioritized to help women avoid unplanned pregnancies. Retention of healthcare staff, particularly in rural or remote areas, is critical. Policies should be developed to create a supportive environment for recruiting, retaining, and motivating personnel in these settings. Strengthening linkages and referral systems is essential, especially for community-based treatment programs, which must be connected to regular care at health facilities with adequate laboratory, diagnostic, and supply management systems. An efficient division of labor among national, regional, and district levels of the health system is crucial to optimize resource use and minimize duplication. Clear roles, responsibilities, and accountability must be established. Expanding ART coverage should be a priority, as all treatment regimens reduce morbidity and mortality. Early diagnosis and prompt ART initiation are particularly critical for infants and young children, who are at higher risk of poor outcomes. Strengthening links between diagnosis and treatment sites is essential to minimize loss to follow-up and improve ART uptake among children. Efforts should be made to optimize the availability of child-friendly ARV formulations, such as scored, dispersible fixed-dose combinations, to support ART scale-up in remote areas. Regulatory approval of preferred formulations should be accelerated. Countries should phase out the use of d4T in favor of safer alternatives like TDF, which is more effective and less likely to cause resistance. A costed phase-out plan should be developed, including investments in laboratory strengthening and capacity-building. Adequate forecasting and procurement of alternative drugs are critical to avoid stock-outs and treatment disruptions. Monitoring and evaluation systems must be adapted to track the implementation and impact of new guidelines. Data collection should focus on critical outcomes, such as viral suppression, immune reconstitution, and HIV-related mortality, while also monitoring potential unintended outcomes like drug resistance and ARV-related toxicities. Community involvement in monitoring and evaluation is essential to understand the experiences and perceptions of people living with HIV and to design effective interventions. WHO is developing a consolidated guide on monitoring and evaluation of HIV programs to align existing approaches with new recommendations and provide guidance in emerging areas. Finally, scaling up viral load monitoring is crucial to identify treatment failure and avoid unnecessary switches to second-line regimens. As ART programs expand, monitoring service quality and strengthening linkages across the care cascade will be essential to optimize treatment outcomes and long-term program performance.
